questions.q: What is the first question a threat model answers?
options: Did we do a good enough job?
What are we building?
What are we going to do about it?
Who is on the response team?
questions.explain: Threat modeling starts by diagramming the system — "what are we building" — because the diagram is what reveals where risk actually concentrates.

options: A firewall rule written in YAML
A point in a system where the level of trust changes, such as between the public internet and an internal network
A legal agreement between a company and a cloud vendor
The maximum number of users allowed on a system
questions.explain: A trust boundary marks where trust level changes in a data flow diagram — for example, where a customer's browser on the public internet meets Northbridge's checkout service.

questions.q: In STRIDE, which category covers an attacker viewing data they shouldn't have access to?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Information disclosure
Denial of service
questions.explain: Information disclosure in STRIDE covers unauthorized visibility into data, such as a misconfigured database exposing another customer's order history.

questions.q: A bug lets a regular Northbridge Retail customer reach an admin-only order-adjustment endpoint. Which STRIDE category does this describe?
options: Repudiation
Elevation of privilege
Denial of service
Spoofing
questions.explain: Gaining capabilities beyond what was intended — a customer reaching an admin-only function — is elevation of privilege.

questions.q: Why is threat modeling described as cheapest when done before code is written?
options: Because it is legally required before writing any code
Because design-time changes are far less costly than reworking an already-deployed architecture
Because threat modeling tools only work on whiteboards
Because code written after a threat model never contains vulnerabilities
questions.explain: Changing a design decision on a whiteboard is cheap. Making the same change after a service is already deployed requires a much larger rework — the shift-left argument applied to threat modeling.
